hints: Suppose you already know which beginnings of text can be split perfectly. How could that knowledge tell you about a slightly longer beginning?
Use DP over prefixes: ok[i] means the first i letters can be split. From every i with ok[i] true, walk a trie of the dictionary along text; every word end you hit at position j makes ok[j] true.

1. Insert every dictionary word into a trie.
  2. ok[0] = true, all others false.
  3. For i from 0 to n−1, if ok[i]: walk the trie from the root over text[i], text[i+1], …
  4. Stop when the path breaks; whenever the current node ends a word at position j, set ok[j+1] = true.
  5. Return ok[n].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Recursively try every dictionary word that matches at the current position and recurse on the rest; without memo this explodes on inputs like aaaa…b.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Memoised recursion or DP with a hash set: for each end i try every start j and check whether text[j..i) is in the set.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: DP + trie: from each reachable start, walk the trie at most 20 letters (longest word), marking every reachable end.
approaches.time: O(n·L + dictionary letters), L = longest word

explain: Sample "sunflower" with [sun, flow, flower, er]: ok[0] is true. Walking from 0 we hit the end of sun, so ok[3] = true. From 3 we walk f-l-o-w (word end → ok[7]) and then e-r (word end → ok[9]). ok[9] is the full length, so the answer is true; the path sun|flow|er also exists. For catdogs, we reach ok[6] after cat|dog, but no word starts with s, so ok[7] stays false. Invariant: ok[i] is true exactly when the first i letters split perfectly. Edge case: words can be reused, which the DP allows naturally.
recognize: 'Can the string be cut into pieces that all come from a word list?' → prefix DP (word break), with a trie to find matching words fast.
